content: A Taylor cone is a specific conical shape that forms during electrospray and hydrodynamic spray processes when a jet of charged particles is emitted from a liquid surface under the influence of an electric field. This phenomenon occurs when the applied voltage exceeds a certain threshold. The Taylor cone is not only significant in electrospray ionization used in mass spectrometry but also plays a critical role in the operation of colloid thrusters, which are employed for precise and efficient low-power thrust control in spacecraft. The concept of the Taylor cone was first described by Sir Geoffrey Ingram Taylor in 1964, prior to the formal discovery of electrospray. Taylor's work built upon earlier studies, including Zeleny’s 1917 photographic documentation of a cone-jet of glycerine under a high electric field, as well as contributions from Wilson and Taylor (1925), Nolan (1926), and Macky (1931). Taylor’s primary interest lay in understanding the behavior of water droplets in strong electric fields, such as those present in thunderstorms. When a small volume of electrically conductive liquid is subjected to an electric field, the liquid's shape begins to deform from its natural state, which is governed by surface tension alone. As the voltage increases, the electric field exerts a force on the liquid that becomes comparable to the force of surface tension. At this point, the liquid forms a cone with convex sides and a rounded tip. When the voltage reaches a critical threshold, the rounded tip inverts and emits a jet of liquid, a phenomenon known as a cone-jet. This marks the initiation of the electrospray process, during which ions can transition into the gas phase. To maintain a stable cone-jet, the applied voltage must slightly exceed the threshold value. Further increases in voltage can lead to other modes of droplet disintegration. The term Taylor cone can refer specifically to the theoretical ideal of a perfect cone with a precise angle or more generally to the approximately conical region of a cone-jet after the electrospray process has begun. Taylor demonstrated that the shape of the cone approaches the theoretical ideal just before jet formation. The angle of this cone is known as the Taylor angle, which is mathematically defined as π θ₀, where θ₀ is the first zero of the Legendre polynomial of order 1/2, P₁/₂(cos θ₀). This angle is approximately 49.3°. Taylor's derivation of the cone's shape is based on two key assumptions: (1) the surface of the cone is an equipotential surface, and (2) the cone exists in a steady-state equilibrium. To satisfy these conditions, the electric field must exhibit azimuthal symmetry and have a dependence proportional to √R to counteract surface tension and produce the cone. The solution to this problem involves an equipotential surface (V = V₀) existing at a specific value of θ₀, regardless of the radial distance (R), thereby forming an equipotential cone. The complement of this angle is the Taylor angle.
